candidates.title: Compare supplier confirmations with purchase orders

demandEvidence.chore: Manually compare each supplier confirmation’s SKU, quantity, price and delivery date against the purchase order.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: When a supplier confirmation contains dozens of line items, manually comparing every SKU, quantity, price, and delivery date against the original Purchase Order becomes time-consuming.

ease.reason: Synthetic purchase-order and confirmation rows make a comparison test startable, but the source documents no accessible tool or format.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: ecommerce operators may pay to reduce manual supplier-order checks; the discussion establishes no buyer or payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock can flag differences in operator-supplied tables; varied documents and match accuracy need human review.

autonomy.reason: A proposed comparison can flag mismatches, but an operator must provide records and verify every discrepancy; no matching implementation reference is supplied.

evidence.reason: The post names manual comparison of SKU, quantity, price and delivery date, but gives no frequency or corroboration.

candidates.reason: A bounded synthetic-table comparison is assessable from this concrete chore, but no supplied implementation reference supports its automation and its provisional mean is below 6.

candidates.title: Draft clearer order status updates

demandEvidence.chore: Prepare customer-facing order status updates when internal operational data is incomplete or changes frequently.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I’d be interested to hear how others handle customer-facing status updates when internal operational data is incomplete or changes frequently.

ease.reason: A small test can use operator-supplied order-status fields, but no supplied implementation reference supports a working integration.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: ecommerce operators might pay for clearer order updates; this community request proves neither payment nor a service market.

feasibility.reason: A four-week mock could draft an update from synthetic status fields; missing data, store access and factual accuracy require human checks.

autonomy.reason: A proposed draft loop could format supplied status details, but a person must resolve gaps and approve each customer message; no matching reference is supplied.

evidence.reason: The post asks about customer-facing status updates when operations data is incomplete or changes; recurrence and exact fields are unspecified.

candidates.reason: The stated update problem supports a narrow draft-only experiment, but limited task detail and no implementation reference leave the provisional mean below threshold.

candidates.title: Notify a restaurant when a web order arrives

demandEvidence.chore: Build an automated notification system for new restaurant website orders.
demandEvidence.evidenceQuote: I want to build an automated restaurant order notification system using Make.com .

ease.reason: A mock can turn operator-supplied test orders into alert text, but no supplied reference supports an order trigger or WhatsApp delivery.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: small restaurants may pay for timely order alerts; this request establishes neither a buyer market nor payment.

feasibility.reason: A four-week test can format synthetic orders into alerts; connecting a real website and messaging account is unverified and needs permission.

autonomy.reason: The proposed loop formats a supplied order into a notification, but trigger delivery and message sending lack implementation evidence and need human checks.

evidence.reason: The request explicitly seeks automated restaurant order notifications, but gives no frequency, order fields, or corroboration.

candidates.reason: A narrow synthetic-order alert mock can be assessed from the concrete request, but the trigger and WhatsApp delivery are unsupported by supplied implementation evidence and the provisional mean is below 6.
